{{short description|Mathematical tool in crystallography}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2017}}
{{Use British English|date=February 2017}}
[[File:Beevers-Lipson strips at the Museum of the History of Science, Oxford.JPG|thumb|Beevers–Lipson strips at the [[Museum of the History of Science, Oxford]],<ref name="mhs" /> part of the ''Crystals'' special exhibition in 2014. These were used by the [[Nobel Prize]] winner [[Dorothy Hodgkin]] in Oxford.]]

'''Beevers–Lipson strips''' were a computational aid for early [[Crystallography|crystallographers]] in calculating [[Fourier transform]]s to determine the structure of [[crystal]]s from crystallographic data,<ref name="beevers-lipson">{{cite journal| title=A Brief History of Fourier Methods in Crystal-structure Determination | first1=C. A. | last1=Beevers | authorlink1=C. Arnold Beevers | first2=H. | last2=Lipson | authorlink2=Henry Lipson | journal=[[Australian Journal of Physics]] | volume=38 | pages=263–271 | year=1985 | issue=3 | bibcode=1985AuJPh..38..263B | doi=10.1071/ph850263| doi-access=free }}</ref> enabling the creation of models for complex molecules.<ref name="gould">{{cite web| url=http://www.iucr.org/news/newsletter/volume-8/number-3/beevers-lipson-strips | title=The mechanism of Beevers–Lipson strips | first=Bob | last=Gould | work=BCA Newsletter | volume=8 | number=3 | date=December 1998 | publisher=[[International Union of Crystallography]] | accessdate=28 March 2014 }}</ref> They were used from the 1930s<ref name="mhs" /> until computers with enough power became generally available in the 1960s.

The technique was developed by [[C. Arnold Beevers]] (1908–2001),<ref name="beevers">{{cite web | url=http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/obits_alpha/beevers_cecil.pdf | title=Cecil Arnold Beevers | work=Crystallography News | publisher=[[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] | year=2001 | accessdate=28 March 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140329014642/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/obits_alpha/beevers_cecil.pdf | archive-date=29 March 2014 | url-status=dead }}</ref> reader in [[crystallography]] at the [[University of Edinburgh]], and [[Henry Lipson]] CBE [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (1910–1991), Professor of [[Physics]] at the [[University of Manchester Institute of Science and Technology]]. The approach converted the sizable calculations of multi-dimensional Fourier summations needed in crystallography analysis into sums of more manageable one-dimensional values.<ref name="gould" /> The folded card strips with numbers were typically stored in two wooden boxes,<ref name="harvard">{{cite web | url=http://dssmhi1.fas.harvard.edu/emuseumdev/code/emuseum.asp?emu_action=searchrequest&newsearch=1&moduleid=1&profile=objects&currentrecord=1&searchdesc=Beevers-Lipson%20strips%20in%20oak%20case&style=single&rawsearch=id/,/is/,/1172/,/false/,/true | title=Beevers–Lipson strips in oak case | work=Collection of Historical Scientific Instruments | publisher=[[Harvard University]] | location=USA | accessdate=28 March 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140329014117/http://dssmhi1.fas.harvard.edu/emuseumdev/code/emuseum.asp?emu_action=searchrequest&newsearch=1&moduleid=1&profile=objects&currentrecord=1&searchdesc=Beevers-Lipson%20strips%20in%20oak%20case&style=single&rawsearch=id%2F%2C%2Fis%2F%2C%2F1172%2F%2C%2Ffalse%2F%2C%2Ftrue | archive-date=29 March 2014 | url-status=dead }}</ref> one for [[sine]]s<ref name="mhs">{{cite web| url=http://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/collections/imu-search-page/record-details/?TitInventoryNo=80368&querytype=field&thumbnails=on&irn=15017 | title=Set of Beevers Lipson Strips, Sine Set, c.1936 | publisher=[[Museum of the History of Science]] | location=Oxford | number=80368 | accessdate=28 March 2014 }}</ref> and one for [[cosine]]s. Previously it was necessary to consult sine/cosine tables, a time-consuming process. The approach was used by the [[Nobel Prize]] winner [[Dorothy Hodgkin]] OM FRS (1910–1994).<ref name="mhs" /><ref name="hodgkin">{{cite web| url=http://gos.sbc.edu/h/ch/ch.html | title=Nobel Lecture: The X-Ray Analysis Of Complicated Molecules | first=Dorothy Crowfoot | last=Hodgkin | work=Chemistry, Nobelstiftelsen | location=Amsterdam | publisher=[[Elsevier]] | pages=70–94 | date=11 December 1964 | accessdate=28 March 2014 }}</ref> The technique was used in computer programs until the invention of the [[fast Fourier transform]].<ref name="november">{{cite book| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-cIdzHlhGYgC&pg=PA30 | title=Biomedical Computing: Digitizing Life in the United States | first=Joseph A. | last=November | page=30 | publisher=[[Johns Hopkins University Press]] | year=2012 | isbn=9781421404684 | accessdate=28 March 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Watkin |first1=David J. |title=Chemical crystallography–science, technology or a black art |journal=Crystallography Reviews |date=2010 |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=197–230 |doi=10.1080/08893110903483246 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/08893110903483246 |access-date=8 September 2025}}</ref>
